summary: Part 2, Indigenous-authored history and critique (Agent B). The field indigenous is relabelled 'Indigenous-authored history & critique', its description, figures, scope note, date label and date span are rewritten for authorship-based membership, its coverage set to 2017, and its chronology grows from 9 to 25 events (1944–2017). Two strands are added (refusal_resurgence; peoplehood) and four corrected (Hawaiian historical authority with the 1991 Trask–Keesing–Linnekin exchange; Métis criticism of representation with LaRocque's named targets; McNickle's institutions; Deloria's criticism). Five person entries: Audra Simpson (5 edges, 11 events), Glen Sean Coulthard (5, 6), Emma LaRocque (4, 5), Chris Andersen (2, 5; plus Agent A's ihA_rel_06) and Haunani-Kay Trask (3, 8). Linda Tuhiwai Smith (chronology 1 → 16 events) and D'Arcy McNickle (2 → 12 events; edge_775 evidence revised) are backfilled. On settler_colonialism (correction C3) the strand recognition_refusal_resurgence now says what Coulthard, Audra Simpson and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson each target, and four roster rows are corrected. The Decolonizing Methodologies source links are set to the publisher's DOI. Fourteen source records added and six amended; two people records added (chris_andersen, taiaiake_alfred) and identity notes sourced for nine people records.
rationale: Research of 2026-10-27: data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md (Agent B: readings §§1.1–1.12; proposals §§2.1–2.12). Every stage-1 edge rests on the author's own words in a text read, or on a named reader's explicit statement read (Nicoll 2015; Kauanui 2016; Beck 1995; Iverson 1993); 'as quoted by' passages are marked and never carry an edge alone. The fragment's ihB_rel numbers supersede the provisional numbering in the evidence file. Identity notes rest on the author's own words or a publisher or institutional profile (rule 9); no one is included because of identity. Coordinator decisions applied: the five stage-1 entries; Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Moreton-Robinson and Kameʻeleihiwa as roster rows only (stage 2 entries); McNickle's birth year only; C3 accepted; reviewed_through 2017. Decolonizing Methodologies: url set on smith_decolonizing and promotion01_smith to https://doi.org/10.5040/9781350225282, the publisher's (Zed Books/Bloomsbury) DOI for the 2021 edition, found through Crossref; the 1999 Zed edition has no DOI and the Bloomsbury product page refused automated access; the reading notes are kept unchanged. B creates the chris_andersen node and people record, which A's ihA_rel_06 uses as its source; A should not create a second record. Edges needed from Agent A (they end in A's fields): ihA_rel_06 chris_andersen → native_newcomer/fur_trade_families_metis (A's id; my introduction pages 10–12 and 20 can be added to its evidence); ihA_rel_09 michael_witgen → indigenous, accepted for part 2 as A drafted it (not duplicated here); requested: audra_simpson → ethnohistory (critique: 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm', 2007 pp. 70–71), emma_larocque → native_newcomer target_strand historians_indian (critique of Walker's survey, 1999 PDF p. 119) and target_strand contact_wendat_representation (Trigger's foreword to Sioui, PDF pp. 135–136), darcy_mcnickle → ethnohistory (the Newberry centre, Iverson 1993 p. v). edge_1003 (indigenous → sylvia_van_kirk) is left as A proposes; if LaRocque's entry is accepted, its source could later be set to emma_larocque. The Shekon Neechie open letter (2021; A's source iha_shekon_neechie_2021) belongs on the indigenous chronology as a context event if A's source record is merged; not added here to avoid a dangling reference. Strand moves out of indigenous are A's and C's; B moves nothing. Held for OCAP review (user rules of 2026-10-27; removed from or never placed in fragment text): (1) the Hawaiian time concept that Trask quotes from Kameʻeleihiwa (1991, p. 164), formerly in the Hawaiian strand, Trask's description and edge, and Kameʻeleihiwa's row; (2) Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's account of Elders as historians and of an Elder's oral history of the Michi Saagiig and the 1923 treaty (2014, pp. 13, 19–20), and the names of the community reviewers in her n. 1; (3) McNickle's descent and his mother's ancestry as described by Iverson (1993, p. xv): his identity note and text now say only 'enrolled member at Flathead (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes), per Iverson 1993' (OCAP review #3); (4) first-person or ancestral identity phrasings (Smith's 2022 self-introduction, LaRocque's dissertation sentence, Coulthard's and Audra Simpson's self-descriptions, Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's ancestry wording and the passage on the women of her family (her note keeps 'Michi Saagiig Nishnaabeg, Alderville First Nation', OCAP review #4), Smith's birthplace and former surname): identity notes now give the nation or community as publicly stated, with one source; identity labels are removed from descriptions and roster contexts; (5) Audra Simpson's interview passages and the details of Kahnawà:ke membership disputes (2007, pp. 72–78): only her published argument about colonial membership law is described; (6) the 1975 Dene Declaration as a chronology event for Coulthard (dropped); (7) Andersen's description of Brenda Macdougall's identity (now 'the historian'). Retained after review (OCAP review #7): Trask's argument that genealogy is valid historical evidence ('Native forms of history') and her critique of Keesing; her sentence on land in pre-haole Hawaiʻi appears in no fragment text or source note. Chronology events with 'year_range' carry a qualifier.

text_revisions.old: Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and scholarly research meet in varied academic practices. Oral histories, family relationships, archival inquiry and collaborations contribute different resources; authority and methods remain situated.
text_revisions.new: Historical writing, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors, from early manuscript and print witnesses to academic history and political theory. It is plural: Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Dakota, Māori, Hawaiian and Aboriginal traditions have their own roots and are not branches of one academic field. From 1969 Deloria, Adams, LaRocque, Sioui, Trask and Smith turned criticism on the institutions and disciplines that studied them; LaRocque judged that 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999). After 2000 the criticism became theory: Audra Simpson's 'ethnographic refusal' (2007, 2014); Coulthard's case against 'the politics of recognition' (2009, 2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's resurgence, which turns from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (2014); Andersen's Métis 'peoplehood' against 'mixedness' (2014). Older university scholarship about Indigenous peoples and community-engaged research have their own entries; settler colonial studies is a comparative field.

text_revisions.old: Earlier selected writing includes Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), and Cree/Tainui interwar work. Twentieth-century examples include McNickle (1949), Deloria (1969), Adams and LaRocque (1975), Dickason (1984, 1992), Sioui (1989), Walker (1990), Kameʻeleihiwa (1992), O’Brien (1997), Wilson (1996), and Smith (1999). See the distinct approaches for works, collaborators and evidence limits. Related scholarship includes Miller, White, Harris and Lutz; Stó:lō field-school practice credits community and university participants. Leddy’s 2010 reflection supplies a separately dated later case.
text_revisions.new: Earlier witnesses: Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), Warren (1885), Thunderchild and Ahenakew (1923; 1929), Pei Te Hurinui Jones (1929), Mathews (1932, 1961), Te Rangi Hīroa (1938, 1949), McNickle (1949; Native American Tribalism, 1973). Critiques 1969–99: Deloria, Custer Died for Your Sins (1969); Adams, Prison of Grass (1975); LaRocque, Defeathering the Indian (1975) and her dissertation (1999); Dickason (1984, 1992); Sioui (1989); Walker (1990); Trask, 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991) and From a Native Daughter (1993); Kameʻeleihiwa (1992); Wilson (1996); O'Brien (1997); Rigney (1999); Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (1999). After 2000: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) and Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Coulthard, Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017); Andersen, 'Métis' (2014); Moreton-Robinson, The White Possessive (2015). See the strands for works, collaborators and evidence limits.

text_revisions.old: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples.
text_revisions.new: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples. In 1991 Trask answered Keesing's charge that Pacific nationalists 'invent' their pasts: genealogy is 'solid evidence from Native forms of history', and Hawaiians do not want 'to be "liberated" from our past'. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'.

text_revisions.old: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions.
text_revisions.new: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions. The dissertation names its targets: James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing ('Canadian historiography is not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui as 'a language of containment', and the 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk; Adams is her 'Metis historian and social critic' (PDF pp. 47, 119, 135–136, 249). When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.

text_revisions.old: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge.
text_revisions.new: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge. His 1973 preface challenged administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. He helped found the NCAI (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and directed the Newberry centre in its first fellowship year (1973–74).

text_revisions.new: Deloria’s manifesto supplies a distinct Native American intervention; specific chapters remain to be read. As a guest speaker in 1965 he criticised the McNickle-organised workshops (Beck 1995, mediated); Audra Simpson cites Custer with Asad and Said for anthropology's place in empire (2007, n. 2).

text_revisions.new: Her 1999 dissertation relates her 1974 research on stereotypes in Alberta history and social-studies texts to Defeathering the Indian and names its targets in Canadian historiography: Walker's survey ('not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui ('a language of containment') and the cross-cultural approach of Brown and Van Kirk. Distinct from Adams, on whom she draws.

text_revisions.old: Earlier historical synthesis and institution-building: the Newberry finding aid records his 1949 work and participation in creating its history centre in 1972. Institutional and bibliographic evidence does not establish particular book arguments or a universal field foundation.
text_revisions.new: A writer, administrator and historian, an enrolled member at Flathead (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes), per Iverson 1993. He helped found the National Congress of American Indians (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and chaired the steering committee of the 1961 Chicago conference. They Came Here First (1949) and Native American Tribalism (1973) argued against 'the certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress': Congress in the 1950s had judged that 'Indians had no future as Indians', and termination tried 'to legislate Indians out of existence'. In 1972 he helped create the Newberry Library's centre for Indian history and directed it in its first fellowship year (1973–74). Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. Vine Deloria Jr. criticised the workshops' approach in 1965.

field_sets.expect: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.
field_sets.value: Part 2 of the Indigenous histories family (split in revision 1.201): history, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors. Membership rests on Indigenous authorship or co-authorship sourced person by person, in the author's own words or an institutional or publisher profile (see the people records), never inferred from a name or a topic. Collaborative and community-directed research has its own entry; settler scholarship about Indigenous peoples is in Ethnohistory and Indigenous–newcomer relations; settler colonial studies is a comparative field. Reviewed through 2017. Read in full: Audra Simpson 2007; Trask 1991 with Keesing's reply; Nicoll's 2015 review of Simpson and Moreton-Robinson. Read in part: Coulthard's 2009 dissertation; Leanne Betasamosake Simpson 2014; Andersen 2009 and the introduction of 2014; LaRocque 1999; Iverson's 1993 introduction to McNickle. Known through named readers or publishers only: Mohawk Interruptus, Red Skin, White Masks, The White Possessive, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back, As We Have Always Done, Native Land and Foreign Desires. Works of 2018–24 are not yet surveyed. In Canadian History PhDs Smith is cited by 47, Audra Simpson by 34, Coulthard by 27 and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson by 26, the last three from almost none before 2010 (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).

strand.title: Refusal, resurgence and the critique of recognition
strand.focus: Three linked but distinct arguments, each with its own target. Audra Simpson proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus (2014) carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's history and Morgan and Parker's ethnology. Coulthard challenged 'the now commonplace assumption' that colonial relations in Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon against Taylor and reworking Marx: 'dispossession, not proletarianization' shaped Indigenous–state relations (2009; book 2014). Leanne Betasamosake Simpson defined resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and met the academy's 'colonial refusal' with 'Indigenous refusal' (2014), citing Coulthard on recognition and Simpson on refusal. Alfred's Wasáse (2005) is a shared reference. In the pages read none of them criticises Wolfe.
strand.works: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007), Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Glen Sean Coulthard, Subjects of Empire? (PhD, 2009), Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017)

strand.title: Peoplehood against mixedness
strand.focus: Andersen argues that Métis are misrecognised 'as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'. To the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us'. Peoplehood rests on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood' (2014). His 2009 essay asks Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using disciplines including history. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall.
strand.works: Chris Andersen, 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014)
